title: Do Nows: Must They Activate Prior Knowledge?
author: Salles, Dominic
summary: Using the mathematics of the forgetting curve, this piece argues that spaced retrieval practice in a lesson's opening 'Do Now' should almost always take priority over activating prior knowledge specifically relevant to that day's lesson, because the volume of retrieval a knowledge curriculum actually requires (the author calculates roughly 1,350 retrieval questions per year, or about 23 per lesson) cannot be accommodated any other way, and skipping the correctly-spaced retrieval produces catastrophic memory loss according to the curve's own formulae. The counterargument that this makes lessons feel robotic is addressed directly with a worked example: a Macbeth essay with quotation gaps students fill from memory functions simultaneously as spaced retrieval and prior-knowledge activation, showing the choice needn't be fully binary in well-designed tasks. The piece also argues prior-knowledge activation for a specific lesson is less urgent than commonly assumed, since a well-connected curriculum re-activates related content naturally through weekly recurrence, whereas content not currently being taught (a previously studied novel, for instance) has no such natural reinforcement and will be lost catastrophically without deliberate spaced retrieval.
points: The forgetting curve's own formulae predict catastrophic memory loss when retrieval intervals are missed, and the volume of retrieval a real knowledge curriculum requires (calculated here at roughly 1,350 questions per year, ~23 per lesson) can only be fit into class time via Do Nows, not homework alone.

When forced into a binary choice, the argument favors spaced retrieval of previously taught content over activating prior knowledge specific to the day's lesson, because the consequence of missing spaced retrieval is a 'TNT sized' memory loss while missing lesson-specific activation is comparatively minor.

A worked classroom example shows the choice needn't be fully binary: a Macbeth essay with quotation gaps filled from memory functions as spaced retrieval and lesson-relevant prior-knowledge activation simultaneously.

Activating prior knowledge specific to a given lesson is argued to be less critical than commonly assumed, since a well-connected curriculum re-activates recurring content naturally through weekly exposure — the real risk is content that isn't currently being taught and has no such natural reinforcement.

Knowledge organisers are reframed as fundamentally retrieval-planning documents: 'The knowledge organiser is how you plan retrieval. That's precisely and only what it is for' — meaning they should be ruthlessly limited to only what must be retrieved.
quotes: No, I don't think so. If we start with the forgetting curve, it predicts that knowledge will be forgotten unless it is retrieved at the best spaced intervals.
When we look at the required spacings of these retrievals we simply cannot fit them in if we don't use Do Nows.
Activating Prior Knowledge is Not That Important Anyway. This is because the curriculum activates prior knowledge all the time.

I give them a grade 7 essay on a Macbeth question, but with gaps for each of the quotes... This activates their prior knowledge in a purposeful way, while they are actually learning so much more from the structure and vocabulary of the essay itself.
Total Retrieval Questions for the Year: 1,350... that's about 23 Do Now Questions per lesson. Most teachers would never dream of a 10 question Do Now, never mind a 23.
The knowledge organiser is how you plan retrieval. That's precisely and only what it is for.
Whichever way you peel this onion, ignoring the spacing in your Do Now so you can activate prior knowledge is only going to end one way: tears (because students will forget).
